0.title: Malachi: The Sun of Righteousness
0.overview:
The message. Malachi is God’s word to people who still came to worship but had stopped expecting anything from him. The temple had been rebuilt, the sacrifices went on, and it had all gone flat: “What a weariness this is” (1:13). God’s first word to them is not a rebuke but a declaration: “I have loved you,” says the LORD (1:2). Then, answering their every objection, he exposes what their tiredness had hidden: careless worship, broken marriages, withheld tithes, and the suspicion that serving him does not pay. And he promises to come himself, sending his messenger ahead of him, to refine his people and to make plain at last the difference between those who serve him and those who do not.

Background: the writer. We know nothing about Malachi except his name, which means “my messenger”. It fits a book full of messengers: the priest “is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (2:7), and God promises, “Behold, I send my messenger” (3:1). So some readers, from the ancient Greek translation onwards, have taken “Malachi” as a title drawn from 3:1 rather than a personal name, and one old Jewish tradition identified the writer with Ezra. But every other book of the Twelve opens with its prophet’s name, and this commentary takes Malachi as the name of a real prophet through whom God spoke.

When and where. The Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC. After Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, exiles came home, and, stirred by Haggai and Zechariah, finished a new temple in 516 or 515 BC. Malachi gives no date, but the temple is standing and its sacrifices are offered (1:10), Judah answers to a Persian “governor” (1:8), and the sins he attacks are the very ones Nehemiah found: corrupt priests, marriages to worshippers of other gods, and tithes withheld until the Levites went back to their fields (Nehemiah 13:10–29). So he probably preached about 450 to 430 BC, perhaps when Nehemiah came back from the Persian court to find his reforms undone (Nehemiah 13:6–7). He was the last of the Old Testament prophets; after him came some four centuries with no new prophet’s book.

The first hearers. Judah was a small province, Jerusalem a modest town, and the harvests poor (3:11). The people were not bowing to idols; they were disappointed with God. The priests offered blind, lame and sick animals they would never have dared give the governor (1:8). Men married women who worshipped other gods, and some had been faithless to the wives of their youth (2:11–16). Many had concluded, “It is vain to serve God” (3:14). Yet there was a faithful few: “those who feared the LORD spoke with one another” (3:16).

How to read it. The book calls itself “the oracle of the word of the LORD” (1:1). It is prophecy, mostly in forceful prose rather than the poetry of the earlier prophets, and it is cast as an argument. God makes a statement; the people answer back, “But you say”; God replies. Read it as a debate in which God takes his people’s objections seriously enough to answer every one, and listen for your own voice among the objectors.

How the book makes its case. There are six disputes. First, God’s love (1:1–5): when they ask how he has loved them, he points to his free choice of Jacob over his elder brother Esau, “Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated” (1:2–3), the Bible’s language of choosing and passing over. Second, the priests (1:6–2:9) despise his name with worthless offerings, though “I am a great King” (1:14); beside them stands the faithful priest of old, who “turned many from iniquity” (2:6). Third, faithlessness (2:10–16): to God, by marrying “the daughter of a foreign god” (2:11), and to the wife of one’s youth, a covenant at which “the LORD was witness” (2:14). Fourth, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17–3:5): he is coming to refine his people “like gold and silver” (3:3). Fifth, robbery (3:6–12): “For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed” (3:6), so return to him, and bring the tithe. Sixth, “It is vain to serve God” (3:13–4:3): God keeps “a book of remembrance” (3:16), and a day is coming that will burn the arrogant like stubble but rise on those who fear him like the sun. The book closes (4:4–6) by pointing back to the law of Moses and forward to Elijah, who will turn the hearts of fathers and children. (Hebrew Bibles number chapter 4 as 3:19–24.)

Two passages often misused. “Put me to the test” (3:10) is God’s word to a farming nation under the covenant of Moses, promising rain and harvests; the tithe fed the Levites and the poor. It teaches that God notices what we do with money and is lavishly generous, not that givers will be repaid in cash. This commentary’s view is that the New Testament commands no fixed percentage but giving that is regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful; a tenth is a good benchmark, not a ceiling or a debt. The Hebrew of 2:16 is difficult: older versions read “he hates divorce”, while the ESV speaks of “the man who does not love his wife but divorces her”. Either way it condemns the treachery of a man who discards a faithful wife; God takes her side, and the verse is no club for those whose marriages have already broken. This commentary holds, with the Reformed confessions, that Scripture allows divorce for adultery or desertion, and that persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion.

Where it leads: to Christ. Malachi leads to Christ above all by promise. Jesus said of John the Baptist, “This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you’” (Matthew 11:10). In Malachi the messenger prepares the way before the LORD himself; so when Jesus came to the temple, as a baby in Simeon’s arms and later to cleanse it, the Lord had come to his temple. The angel told the priest Zechariah that his son would go before him “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17), and Jesus said, “he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14). Zechariah sang that “the sunrise shall visit us from on high” (Luke 1:78), the sun of righteousness rising with healing. The book also exposes a need. Priests who could not keep the covenant of Levi point to the one high priest “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26). And the Old Testament ends with a curse still hanging over the land, until “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). When Moses and Elijah, the book’s last two names, appeared with Jesus on the mountain, the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5).

For us. Malachi speaks to believers who keep going but have stopped expecting much. God’s first word is still “I have loved you”, and in Christ the proof is not our circumstances but his choice, for “he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4), and his cross. The book searches us: do we give God our leftovers, keep faith with husband or wife, handle money as his, or serve him only for what we get? It also encourages: the ordinary conversations of believers who hold on in a discouraging time are written in God’s book, and they will be his “treasured possession” (3:17). We live after the sunrise Malachi promised, and we wait for the day when the Lord who came will come again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — How Have You Loved Us?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s first word to a disappointed people is love, and his proof is his own free choice. When they ask, “How have you loved us?”, he takes them back to two brothers: Esau was the elder, yet God chose Jacob (vv. 1–3). Edom may vow to rebuild its ruins, but human determination cannot undo what God has decided (v. 4). When Israel sees it, the right response is not boasting but worship: “Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel!” (v. 5). The section lays the foundation of the whole book: every rebuke that follows is spoken by a God who has already loved them.
verseByVerse.theology: God's love for his people rests on his own choice, not on anything in them, and it is visible in their history.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi. "I have loved you," says the LORD. But you say, "How have you loved us?" "Is not Esau Jacob's brother?" declares the LORD. "Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated. I have laid waste his hill country and left his heritage to jackals of the desert." If Edom says, "We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins," the LORD of hosts says, "They may build, but I will tear down, and they will be called 'the wicked country,' and 'the people with whom the LORD is angry forever.'" Your own eyes shall see this, and you shall say, "Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s first word to his tired people is not a rebuke but “I have loved you”, and the proof he gives is his free choice of Jacob over Esau. Why are you here at all, complaining about your harvest? Because I chose your father Jacob when there was no reason to.

By Malachi. The name means “my messenger” (ESV note), fitting a book about messengers that ends by promising the greatest of them (3:1).

But you say. Six times God makes a statement, the people answer back, and God replies. But you say is the drumbeat of Malachi: an argument with a congregation that thinks it has a case.

I have loved you. Everything else in the book stands on these four words: the rebukes that follow are a lover’s, not a judge’s looking for a reason to leave.

How have you loved us? Look at the life we are living, they reply: a small province, a modest temple, poor harvests, foreign governors. Where is this love? It is the question of every disappointed believer: not “Is there a God?” but “Does he love me, given all this?”

Is not Esau Jacob’s brother? God answers by taking them back before either nation existed, to two brothers in one womb (Genesis 25:23). Esau was the elder, with every natural right, and God chose Jacob, the younger, the schemer.

I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated. Hard language, to be handled carefully. In the Bible the pair “love” and “hate” is often the language of choosing and passing over: Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah”, and the next verse says Leah “was hated” (Genesis 29:30–31). Jesus used the same pattern when he said that anyone who comes to him must “hate his own father and mother” (Luke 14:26), meaning that every other loyalty must come second; Matthew gives the same saying as loving them more than him (Matthew 10:37). God is not describing spite against Esau the man but the fact that he chose Jacob’s line to carry his promise, and did not choose Edom’s. Paul quotes the verse, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9:13), to teach that God’s choice does not depend on human merit.

They may build, but I will tear down. Edom’s proud determination to rebuild is the pride Obadiah had condemned, and the verdict is the same. Malachi’s hearers could see the ruin for themselves: in the century after Jerusalem fell, Edom’s own hill country was probably overrun by Arab peoples from the desert, and many Edomites were pushed west into southern Judah, later called Idumea. Human resolve cannot outlast God’s decision.

Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel! The conclusion Israel is meant to draw is not smugness but worship, and it reaches past their own borders. God’s greatness is not a local matter, which is the theme of verse 11.

The answer has a face. Christians should hear this personally. If you are in Christ, the answer to “How have you loved me?” is not your circumstances but God’s choosing of you: he “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). And the evidence is now plainer than Edom’s ruins: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). On a week when nothing in your circumstances seems to say that God loves you, the cross still says it.

What it does not mean. The hatred is not blind spite. Verse 4 ties God’s anger to Edom’s wickedness, and the law still told Israel, “You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7). Nor does God’s choosing make his people better than others; Jacob was chosen as the schemer he was.

Where Christians differ: is this the election of nations or of individuals? Malachi speaks of the nations Israel and Edom (v. 4); Paul applies it to the two men, chosen before birth “not because of works but because of him who calls” (Romans 9:11). Many Christians, especially Arminian and Wesleyan, read Paul as speaking of nations chosen for their place in history rather than persons chosen for salvation. This commentary’s view: both levels are true, for the nations came from the two men. With the Reformed confessions, this commentary holds that Paul means persons: he stresses that the choice came before the twins had done anything (Romans 9:11), and the objection he answers next, “Is there injustice on God’s part?” (Romans 9:14), would hardly arise otherwise. Those who read it differently are brothers and sisters.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “jackals” (v. 3) occurs only here, and its meaning is not certain; the King James Version has “dragons”. Most link it to the usual word for jackals, which haunt ruins elsewhere in the prophets; either way Edom’s land is left to wild creatures.
verseByVerse.note: Malachi probably prophesied around 450–430 BC, perhaps in Nehemiah’s time, making him the last of the Old Testament prophets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Polluted Food on My Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship that gives God the leftovers despises the Father and King who loved his people first. God begins with what everyone knows: a son honours his father and a servant his master (v. 6). Yet the priests offer blind, lame and sick animals they would never dare present to the Persian governor, and still expect God’s favour (vv. 7–9). God would rather someone shut the temple doors, for his name will be great among the nations, honoured with a pure offering in every place (vv. 10–11). His own priests, meanwhile, call his service a weariness and cheat on their vows (vv. 12–14). The answer to every calculation of how little will do is who he is: “I am a great King.”
verseByVerse.theology: Worship that costs nothing and gives God the leftovers insults a great King.

verseByVerse.quote: "A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is my fear? says the LORD of hosts to you, O priests, who despise my name. But you say, 'How have we despised your name?' By offering polluted food upon my altar. But you say, 'How have we polluted you?' By saying that the LORD's table may be despised. When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil? And when you offer those that are lame or sick, is that not evil? Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor? says the LORD of hosts. And now entreat the favor of God, that he may be gracious to us. With such a gift from your hand, will he show favor to any of you? says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests despise God’s name by offering him animals they would be ashamed to give a human governor, and then they ask for his favour. They would never treat an earthly official the way they treat the God who is their Father and Master.

Where is my honor? God turns to the clergy with a simple argument: everyone knows a son honours his father and a servant respects his master. If God is both, where is his honour?

O priests, who despise my name. The priests are genuinely baffled: How have we despised your name? They have not despised it deliberately. The sins Malachi exposes are not scandals but the slow, unnoticed slide of people who still turn up.

Polluted food upon my altar. The altar is called the LORD’s table, and the sacrifices his food (compare Leviticus 21:6). God needs no feeding; the picture is of a king served at his own table, where a shabby meal insults the host.

When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil? God’s law required unblemished animals (Leviticus 22:20). The priests were accepting the animals a farmer could not sell, brought to God because they were no use for anything else.

Present that to your governor. Try offering the Persian governor a lame sheep as your taxes and see how it goes. They would never insult a human official the way they insulted God.

With such a gift from your hand. The sarcasm of verse 9 is heavy: go on, ask God to be gracious to us, with that in your hand.

The Son who honoured his Father. “A son honors his father” (v. 6): one Son did so perfectly. “I honor my Father,” Jesus said (John 8:49), and he gave the Father not what was left over but everything, to the cross. The honour these priests withheld he paid in full.

Giving God leftovers. We give God the tired end of the day, the money left after everything else, the attention the phone did not take. Nobody decides to; it simply happens. Leftovers are what we give someone we have stopped believing loves us, so the cure is not guilt but the chapter’s first words, I have loved you (v. 2).

How do I stop giving God leftovers? Put him first. Give him the first hour. Before the news and the messages, a few unhurried minutes in his word and in prayer. Give him your best on the Lord’s Day. Go to bed in good time on Saturday, arrive before the service starts, and sing as if the words were true. Plan your giving first. Set the amount when the money comes in, not when you see what is left: “Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce” (Proverbs 3:9). Ask the governor’s question. Before you do something for God, ask whether you would offer the same to someone you wanted to impress. None of this buys his favour. Christ, the lamb without blemish, has already been offered for us, so we present our bodies, as Paul urges, “as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God” (Romans 12:1), knowing that nothing offered through him is despised.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors, that you might not kindle fire on my altar in vain! I have no pleasure in you, says the LORD of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name will be great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering. For my name will be great among the nations, says the LORD of hosts. But you profane it when you say that the Lord's table is polluted, and its fruit, that is, its food, may be despised. But you say, 'What a weariness this is,' and you snort at it, says the LORD of hosts. You bring what has been taken by violence or is lame or sick, and this you bring as your offering! Shall I accept that from your hand? says the LORD. Cursed be the cheat who has a male in his flock, and vows it, and yet sacrifices to the Lord what is blemished. For I am a great King, says the LORD of hosts, and my name will be feared among the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God would rather the temple were shut than kept open for bored, cheap worship, because his name will be great among the nations and he is a great King.

Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors. A startling wish: that someone would close the temple and stop the services altogether, for I have no pleasure in you. Half-hearted worship is worse than none, because it tells everyone watching that God is not worth much. He would rather have a locked building than a bored one.

My name will be great among the nations. While the priests shuffle sick animals onto the altar, God says that his name will be great from the rising of the sun to its setting, with a pure offering in every place. To a Jew, for whom worship happened at one altar led by one priestly family, this was almost unthinkable. Jesus told the woman at the well the same thing: the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth (John 4:21–23).

A rebuke inside the promise. If you will not honour me, others will. God is never left without worshippers.

What a weariness this is. Here is the heart-condition behind everything: serving God has become a tiresome job, and they snort at it, unable to hide their contempt.

What has been taken by violence. What they brought included stolen animals. It is possible to be generous to God with what was never rightly ours.

Cursed be the cheat. The final case is the worst: a man who has a good animal, promises it to God, and then swaps in a damaged one. He is not poor; he is a cheat.

For I am a great King. Five words answer every calculation about how little we can get away with giving God. The question is never what we can spare but who he is.

Not the leftover of the flock. This chapter, which began with I have loved you, drives us to the one offering that was never blemished. Christ was “a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), and he was not the leftover of the flock but the Father’s beloved Son. And the worship of every place is now gathering around him: a great multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” before the throne and before the Lamb (Revelation 7:9).

Honest about boredom. What a weariness this is is how a person can feel about church and prayer. God knows when we are bored with him, and it is better to admit it to him than to perform.

Why does God feel boring? We have more entertainment than any generation and are more easily bored, and many who drift from faith never decide against God; they simply find him dull beside everything else on offer. But notice where the fault lies. God had not become small. The priests had stopped looking at him, so the altar became a routine and the King a chore. G. K. Chesterton, in Orthodoxy, pictured God saying to the sun every morning what a child says to a parent, “Do it again,” and suggested that God exults in a sameness we are too tired to enjoy, “for we have sinned and grown old, and our Father is younger than we.” Our weariness is a sign of age, not of insight. The cure is not more stimulation but a fresh sight of who he is: the great King (v. 14) who came down to our altar as the offering himself. No one who has really seen that has found it dull.

Where Christians differ: is the “pure offering” the Mass? Roman Catholic teaching, following some early Christian writers, sees in verse 11 the sacrifice of the Mass, offered in every place. Protestants read it as a picture, in the language of Malachi’s day, of the nations worshipping God everywhere. This commentary’s view: the New Testament names the offerings of the new age: praise and good works (Hebrews 13:15–16), our bodies (Romans 12:1), and the Gentiles themselves (Romans 15:16). Christ’s sacrifice was offered once for all and is never repeated (Hebrews 10:10–14).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 11 has no verb that fixes the time, so it can be read “my name will be great” (ESV) or “my name is great” (ESV note). Read as future, it promises worldwide worship, fulfilled as the gospel goes to the nations; read as present, it is a deliberate overstatement to shame the priests. The future reading is the more likely.

1.title: I Have Loved You
1.overview:
Where we are. Malachi is the last of the Old Testament prophets, speaking to the small community back from exile in Babylon, generations after the temple was rebuilt (see the introduction). This chapter holds the first of the book’s six disputes between God and his people, about his love, and the opening of the second, about the priests’ worship.

The message. Before God rebukes anything, he says, “I have loved you”, and he proves it not from their circumstances but from his free choice of Jacob. Then he shows what their tired worship has forgotten: he is a Father to be honoured and a great King whose name will be great among the nations. To give him our leftovers is to despise the one who loved us first.

Why it was said. Judah was a small Persian province with a modest temple and poor harvests, and the people read their circumstances as proof that God did not care (see the introduction). The priests, who should have kept worship alive, had let it slide into a routine, offering animals no one else would accept.

How the chapter makes its case. God declares his love and answers their “How?” with two brothers: he chose Jacob and passed over Esau, and Edom’s ruins show that his decision stands (vv. 1–5). Then he turns to the priests. A son honours his father, yet they offer blind, lame and sick animals they would never give the governor (vv. 6–9). God would rather someone shut the temple doors, for his name will be great among the nations, with a pure offering in every place (vv. 10–11), while his own priests call his service a weariness and cheat on their vows. But he is a great King (vv. 12–14).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need it exposes. The love that chose Jacob is the love with which God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4), and the worship “in every place” began when the gospel went out to the nations (John 4:21–23). And priests who offered blemished animals point to the one offering God could fully accept: Christ, “a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), not the leftover of the flock but the beloved Son, given by the Father himself.

For us. When faith grows tired, start where God starts: he has loved you, and in Christ the proof is his choice and his cross, not your circumstances. Then ask what you are giving him: the first and best, or what is left when everything else has had its share.
1.theology:
God's love for his people rests on his own choice rather than on anything in them, and the evidence of it is not their circumstances but his electing grace; human determination cannot outlast his decision (vv. 2-4).

Worship that gives God what we would not dare give an earthly official despises his name, and half-hearted worship is worse than none (vv. 6-10). He will be worshipped by the nations in every place, whether or not his own people honour him (v. 11). He sees the weariness behind our routine, and the measure of our giving is not what we can spare but who he is: a great King (vv. 13-14).
1.examples: A congregation argues back six times over, and God answers with two brothers in one womb and a choice made before either had done anything. A lame sheep is offered to God that would never be offered to the tax office, and God wishes someone would lock the doors. Incense rises to him in every place on earth while the temple sulks, its worshippers snort at the service, and a man vows the good animal and swaps in the damaged one.

keyVerse.quote: “I have loved you,” says the LORD. But you say, “How have you loved us?”
keyVerse.note: God’s first word in the last book of the prophets is love, spoken to people who no longer believed it. Every rebuke in the chapter, and in the book, is spoken by this God, and the people’s reply shows the disappointment he is answering. In Christ the answer to their question is no longer only Jacob’s election but the cross (Romans 5:8).

1.reflection:
God answers “How have you loved us?” not by pointing to their circumstances but to his free choice of Jacob (vv. 2–3). When you doubt God’s love, what do you tend to look at? How does the cross change where we look?

The priests offered God what they would never dare give the governor (v. 8). Where are you most tempted to give God the leftovers of your time, money or attention? What would it look like to give him the first and best this week?

“What a weariness this is” (v. 13). Have you ever found worship or prayer boring? What does this chapter suggest is the real cause, and what is the cure?

God says his name will be great among the nations, “in every place” (v. 11). How does knowing that God will be worshipped worldwide, with or without us, humble us and encourage us?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who teach God’s word are his messengers, and when they handle it carelessly they bring the people down with them. God warns the priests that if they will not honour his name he will curse their blessings and shame them before all, so that his covenant with Levi may stand (vv. 1–4). Then he paints the priest he intended: one who feared him, taught truly, walked with him in uprightness and turned many from iniquity, for “the lips of a priest should guard knowledge” (vv. 5–7). These priests have done the opposite, making many stumble and bending their teaching for the influential, and the honour they courted has turned to contempt (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who teach God's word are messengers, and when they corrupt it they bring down the people with them.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O priests, this command is for you. If you will not listen, if you will not take it to heart to give honor to my name, says the LORD of hosts, then I will send the curse upon you and I will curse your blessings. Indeed, I have already cursed them, because you do not lay it to heart. Behold, I will rebuke your offspring, and spread dung on your faces, the dung of your offerings, and you shall be taken away with it. So shall you know that I have sent this command to you, that my covenant with Levi may stand, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God warns careless priests that unless they honour his name, he will turn their blessings into curses and shame them publicly, so that his covenant with Levi may stand.

If you will not take it to heart. Twice: the problem is not ignorance but inattention. They have heard it all, and it has not landed.

I will curse your blessings. The priests’ task was to pronounce blessing over the people (Numbers 6:22–27); now the blessings themselves will turn into curses, and it has already begun.

Spread dung on your faces. Deliberately disgusting. A sacrifice’s dung was carried outside the camp and burned (Exodus 29:14); God will smear it on the faces of the priests who offered it, and they will be carried out with it. Their acceptable worship is, to him, the rubbish from the back of the altar.

That my covenant with Levi may stand. The aim even of this severe word is restoration. God is clearing away what has spoiled the priesthood, and in 3:3 he promises to refine the sons of Levi himself.

No dignity in carelessness. There is no dignity in ministry done carelessly. And since every believer now belongs to “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), the warning reaches anyone who handles holy things half-heartedly.

Uncertain wording. “Offspring” (v. 3) is literally “seed” (ESV note): perhaps the priests’ descendants, perhaps their crops. Some read the same Hebrew letters with different vowels as “arm”, perhaps the shoulder portion of the sacrifices that was the priests’ to eat (Deuteronomy 18:3). Either way, their privileges will turn to disgrace.

verseByVerse.quote: My covenant with him was one of life and peace, and I gave them to him. It was a covenant of fear, and he feared me. He stood in awe of my name. True instruction was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity. For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts. But you have turned aside from the way. You have caused many to stumble by your instruction. You have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the LORD of hosts, and so I make you despised and abased before all the people, inasmuch as you do not keep my ways but show partiality in your instruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets beside the careless priests the priest he intended: one who feared him, taught truly, lived uprightly and turned many from sin, a messenger guarding knowledge for the people. These priests have done the opposite.

My covenant with him was one of life and peace. The covenant God made with Levi brought life and peace, and it produced a man who feared me and stood in awe of my name. Reverence came first; everything else grew from it. Malachi is probably thinking of God’s “covenant of peace” with Aaron’s grandson Phinehas, who was zealous for God’s honour (Numbers 25:10–13), and of Moses’ blessing on Levi, the tribe set apart to teach Israel God’s rules (Deuteronomy 33:8–10).

True instruction was in his mouth. Four marks of a faithful minister follow. True instruction (the ESV notes this may be rendered “law”): what he taught was accurate. No wrong was found on his lips: he did not shade it to please anyone. He walked with me in peace and uprightness: his life matched his teaching. And he turned many from iniquity: real people actually changed.

The lips of a priest should guard knowledge. Like a man entrusted with something valuable that others need. And he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts, the word that gives this book its name: Malachi is God’s messenger, and the priests were meant to be too.

You have caused many to stumble. They show partiality: one ruling for the influential, another for the poor. Teaching that bends for important people corrupts everything.

Despised and abased before all the people. The priests are now despised by the very people they flattered. Honour cannot be bought with compromise.

One has matched it completely. No priest of Levi’s line matched this portrait for long. Jesus has: the high priest who is “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26), in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter 2:22), who showed no partiality and still turns many from iniquity. Where the best human priest could only point to the covenant of life and peace, he is our peace (Ephesians 2:14).

A measure for every teacher. Pastors, Sunday school teachers and parents at the table may all be measured by these four marks, for teachers “will be judged with greater strictness” (James 3:1). And partiality still creeps into churches whenever the generous giver is handled more gently than anyone else (James 2:1–4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — The Wife of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because one God made his people and bound them to himself, faithlessness to one another is faithlessness to him. Malachi turns to the whole community: they share one Father, yet they break faith with each other (v. 10). Some have married women who worship other gods, profaning what God loves, while still bringing their offerings (vv. 11–12). Others drench the altar with tears and cannot understand why God refuses them. The reason is the wife of their youth, betrayed in a covenant at which the LORD was witness (vv. 13–14). God made husband and wife one, seeking godly children, so they must guard themselves in their spirit and not be faithless (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: God is a witness at every wedding, and he takes the breaking of that covenant as seriously as any sin in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Why then are we faithless to one another, profaning the covenant of our fathers? Judah has been faithless, and abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem. For Judah has profaned the sanctuary of the LORD, which he loves, and has married the daughter of a foreign god. May the LORD cut off from the tents of Jacob any descendant of the man who does this, who brings an offering to the LORD of hosts!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because one God made them, his people owe one another faithfulness, and marrying into the worship of another god betrays both him and them.

Have we not all one Father? Malachi turns from the priests to the whole community. Because one God made them his people, faithlessness to each other is an offence against him.

The daughter of a foreign god. The first charge is marriage to women who worship other gods. This is about religion, not race: Israel’s law had always welcomed foreigners who came to trust the God of Israel, and Ruth the Moabite is in the Messiah’s family tree. The problem is marrying into the worship of another god, which is what Ezra and Nehemiah were dealing with at this time (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27).

Who brings an offering to the LORD of hosts! The sting is in the last phrase. The man who does this still comes to worship.

One Father, one family. In Christ the one Father now gathers people from every nation into a single household, “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). That is why the line is drawn at faith, never at race: the family is defined by the Son.

Only in the Lord. The New Testament instinct is the same: a believer is free to marry, “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). This is not snobbery about other people; it is realism about what marriage does to the deepest loyalties of a life.

What it does not mean. It does not tell a Christian already married to an unbeliever to leave. In Ezra’s day the community faced a particular crisis under the old covenant; Paul tells a believer whose unbelieving spouse is willing to stay not to divorce, for the believer’s presence sets the home apart for God (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).

Uncertain wording. “Any descendant” (v. 12) is literally “any who wakes and answers” (ESV note), an obscure idiom. It probably means anyone at all belonging to the man, so that his line is cut off from the community.

verseByVerse.quote: And this second thing you do. You cover the LORD's altar with tears, with weeping and groaning because he no longer regards the offering or accepts it with favor from your hand. But you say, "Why does he not?" Because the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant. Did he not make them one, with a portion of the Spirit in their union? And what was the one God seeking? Godly offspring. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth. "For the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence, says the LORD of hosts. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not be faithless."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God refuses the tearful worship of men who have betrayed the wife of their youth, because marriage is a covenant he himself witnessed; he calls them to guard their hearts and keep faith.

You cover the LORD’s altar with tears. Men weep at the altar because God will not accept their offerings, baffled as to why. The reason is what they have done to their wives. Emotional worship is not the same as acceptable worship. You can weep at the altar and be in the wrong.

The wife of your youth. The wife of your youth: married when they were both young, now set aside for someone else. Your companion: a partner and friend, not a possession. Your wife by covenant: marriage is a covenant, not an arrangement, and the LORD was witness to it. Every wedding has a third party present, God himself.

Did he not make them one? Whatever the difficulties of verse 15, its sense is clear: God made husband and wife one, as Genesis says, “they shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), and he was seeking godly children.

Guard yourselves in your spirit. The command comes twice (the ESV notes it may read “take care”). Faithfulness is guarded on the inside, long before anything happens on the outside, and not by willpower alone: the God who gave a portion of the Spirit to the union gives his Spirit to his people, with his word, prayer and the help of other believers, to keep that guard.

Covers his garment with violence. The man who discards his wife may call it a private matter; God calls it violence, showing on him like blood on his clothing.

The husband who never tires of his bride. Behind every faithful marriage stands a greater one. Paul calls marriage a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32), and Christ is the husband who never tires of his bride. He “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), he has been faithful in every way we have not been, and his faithfulness is counted to us: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). It is both the pattern and the power for ours.

What it does not mean. Scripture does not treat all divorce alike; Jesus allowed for it in some circumstances, and Paul in another, and the Bible everywhere protects the wronged party rather than trapping them. What Malachi condemns is treachery: breaking a covenant because you have tired of the person you made it with. The wife who was sent away is not rebuked here; God takes her side.

For those with broken marriages. Whether you were the betrayer or the betrayed, the book that begins with I have loved you ends with healing in the wings of the sun of righteousness. God takes covenant-breaking seriously because he takes people seriously, and he forgives and restores exactly this.

Shouldn’t I leave if I am no longer happy? To many today that sounds honest, not selfish: if marriage exists to make two people happy, staying in an unhappy one looks like a lie. The sociologist Andrew Cherlin has described how marriage has moved from being the cornerstone of adult life, laid early and built upon, to its capstone, set in place once a person has become who they want to be. Then marriage is a reward for the fulfilled self, and what the self gave, it can take back. Malachi’s men felt the same. The Bible answers with a different kind of love. A contract says, I will stay while you meet my needs. A covenant says, I bind my future to you, and God is witness. That sounds like a cage until you see that it is the only love that can hold you at your worst, and it is God’s love for us. He did not keep us while we pleased him; he bound himself to us by his word and kept it at the cost of his Son.

How do I guard myself in my spirit? The guard goes up at the first small turning of the heart. Watch the first look and the first secret. The private messages, the lingering conversation, the friendship your husband or wife would be uneasy to read about: stop it there. Refuse the comparisons. Turn the thought into thanks for the spouse God gave you: “rejoice in the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5:18). Deal with resentment early. Much treachery grows in a marriage where hurts were stored up rather than spoken and forgiven. Keep investing. Time alone together, kind words, prayer side by side. Let someone ask you. Give a trusted friend permission to ask how your marriage really is. And if you have already failed, do not hide: Christ forgives and restores.

Where Christians differ: is divorce ever allowed, and may a divorced person remarry? Some faithful Christians allow no divorce, or no remarriage while the first spouse lives; others allow divorce for many reasons. This commentary’s view: God hates the treachery of a man who abandons the wife of his youth (v. 16). Jesus allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9), and Paul frees a believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15); the Reformed confessions hold that in those cases the innocent party may remarry (Westminster Confession 24.5–6). Persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion. Anyone being abused should seek safety at once, and the church’s elders should help judge each case and stand with the one wronged. Malachi’s own words point the same way: God condemns the man who covers his garment with violence, not the one who flees it. Divorce on other grounds is sin, but it is not beyond forgiveness in Christ.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 15 and 16 is among the hardest in the book (ESV notes). Verse 15 may mean that God made husband and wife one, as the ESV takes it, or that no one with a remnant of the Spirit would act this way. Verse 16 reads literally “for he hates sending away”, the ordinary idiom for divorce. Older versions took the one who hates to be God (the King James Version has “he hateth putting away”; the ESV margin, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says that he hates divorce”); the ESV text takes it of the man who divorces the wife he does not love. Either way God sets himself against the treachery of discarding a faithful wife.
verseByVerse.note: “Sending away” (v. 16) is the ordinary Hebrew way of speaking of divorce (compare Deut 24:1).

verseByVerse.ref: v. 17 — You Have Wearied the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cynicism about God’s justice wearies him, and his answer is that he is coming. The people have stopped expecting God to act: they say that evildoers please him, or ask with a shrug, “Where is the God of justice?” (v. 17). This is not the honest lament of a Habakkuk, who waited for God’s answer, but the grumbling of people who no longer expect one. The verse opens the fourth dispute, and the reply follows at once in 3:1: the Lord they say they are looking for will suddenly come.
verseByVerse.theology: Cynicism about God's justice wearies him, and his answer is to announce that he is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: You have wearied the LORD with your words. But you say, "How have we wearied him?" By saying, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delights in them." Or by asking, "Where is the God of justice?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people have worn God out with cynical talk, saying that he favours evildoers and asking where his justice is,.

You have wearied the LORD with your words. A striking idea, since God “does not faint or grow weary” (Isaiah 40:28); it shows how deeply this kind of talk grieves him.

Two cynical sayings. First, that God is indifferent to morality: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the LORD. Look around, they said; the crooked prosper and God seems pleased with them. Second, the weary question: Where is the God of justice?

Different from honest lament. This is the complaint of people who have watched injustice go unpunished for a long time. Habakkuk asked “how long?” and stood at his watchpost to wait for an answer (Habakkuk 1:2; 2:1). These men have stopped expecting one; they are simply grumbling.

The answer to come. They asked where the God of justice was. The next verse answers: “Behold, I send my messenger” (3:1). He is coming, and the real question will be who can endure it. He came in Jesus, and the justice they doubted fell, in the end, on him at the cross, where God showed himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

Our version of the question. People still say, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (2 Peter 3:4). The delay is mercy: the Lord “is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9). Bring your complaint to God as lament, and keep watching.

2.title: The Wife of Your Youth
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with God’s charge against priests who offered him blemished animals. This chapter finishes that dispute with a warning to the priests (vv. 1–9), opens the third dispute, about faithlessness (vv. 10–16), and begins the fourth with the people’s cynical question about God’s justice (v. 17).

The message. God takes broken covenants seriously: the covenant he made with Levi, which careless priests have corrupted, and the covenant of marriage, at which he himself was the witness. Those who teach his word must guard it truly and live it, and those who married before him must keep faith with the wife of their youth. Tears at the altar are no substitute for faithfulness at home.

Why it was said. The priests had grown careless and partial in their teaching, and men of Judah were marrying women who worshipped other gods, some apparently discarding their first wives to do it; Nehemiah met the same problems (Nehemiah 13:23–29; see the introduction). Meanwhile the people complained that God seemed to favour the wicked.

How the chapter makes its case. God warns the priests that unless they honour his name he will curse their blessings and shame them publicly (vv. 1–4). Against them he sets his covenant with Levi and the faithful priest who feared God, taught truly, lived uprightly and turned many from iniquity (vv. 5–7), while these priests have made many stumble and shown partiality (vv. 8–9). Then he turns to the people. One God made them all, yet they are faithless to one another, marrying the daughter of a foreign god (vv. 10–12) and abandoning the wife of their youth, so that he refuses their tearful offerings (vv. 13–16). Last, they weary him by asking, “Where is the God of justice?” (v. 17).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by covenant. No priest of Levi’s line lived up to verses 5–7 for long; one has done so completely, Jesus, the high priest “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26). The marriage covenant so lightly broken here pictures the covenant Christ keeps with his bride, for he “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). And the chapter’s last question, “Where is the God of justice?”, is answered in the next verse: the Lord is coming to his temple (3:1).

For us. Those who teach God’s word should measure themselves against the faithful priest, and all of us need the faithful Priest who kept that covenant for us. Guard your heart in your marriage long before anything shows, and where you have failed, come to the Bridegroom who has never broken faith with his bride and who forgives and restores.
2.theology:
God's severest words to his ministers aim at restoring, not abolishing, the ministry (v. 4). A faithful teacher's marks are accurate teaching, integrity, a matching life and people actually turned from sin, while teaching that shows partiality corrupts the covenant and loses the respect it courted (vv. 6-9).

Because one God created us, faithlessness to each other is an offence against him (v. 10). Marriage into the worship of another god profanes what he loves; the issue is religious, not racial (v. 11). Tears at the altar are no substitute for faithfulness at home, for marriage is a covenant at which God himself is the witness (vv. 13-15; Gen 2:24; Matt 19:6), and faithfulness is guarded in the spirit long before anything shows (vv. 15-16). Cynicism about his justice wearies him, and his answer is that he is coming (v. 17).
2.examples: Blessings turn into curses in the mouths of careless priests, and the refuse from the altar is smeared on the faces of those who offered it. A true priest guards knowledge for others; these give one ruling for the influential and another for the poor. An altar is wet with tears and God is not listening, because a third party was present at every wedding and treachery shows on a man like blood on his coat. The chapter ends with people who ask where the God of justice is and no longer expect an answer.

keyVerse.quote: Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Why then are we faithless to one another, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the chapter. Priests who corrupted the covenant of Levi and husbands who betrayed the wife of their youth were guilty of the same sin, faithlessness, and both offended the one God who made them. The faithfulness God asks of his people reflects his own, shown fully in Christ, who keeps covenant with his bride.

2.reflection:
Verses 5–7 describe a faithful priest: reverent, truthful, upright in life, and fruitful in turning people from sin. Which of these marks do you most value in those who teach you? How might they shape the way you teach others, at home or in church?

The men of Judah covered the altar with tears while betraying their wives (vv. 13–14). Why is it possible to be emotional in worship and still be in the wrong? What does God look for instead?

“So guard yourselves in your spirit” (v. 15). What are the small, early turnings of the heart that lead to unfaithfulness, in marriage or in other commitments? What practical guards can we help one another keep?

The people asked, “Where is the God of justice?” (v. 17). How is cynical grumbling different from honest lament? How does the coming of Christ, and his promised return, answer the question?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lord Will Suddenly Come to His Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the question “Where is the God of justice?” by announcing that he is coming himself. A messenger will prepare his way, and then the Lord they say they are seeking will suddenly come to his temple, the messenger of the covenant (v. 1). His coming will be hard to endure, like a refiner’s fire and fullers’ soap, but it aims to purify: he will refine the priests until their offerings please him again (vv. 2–4). Then he will draw near for judgment, a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers and perjurers, against those who cheat workers and wrong the widow, the fatherless and the sojourner, and against all who do not fear him (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: They asked where the God of justice was; he answers that he is coming, and the question is who can stand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming, says the LORD of hosts. But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap. He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD. Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD as in the days of old and as in former years. "Then I will draw near to you for judgment. I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, against the adulterers, against those who swear falsely, against those who oppress the hired worker in his wages, the widow and the fatherless, against those who thrust aside the sojourner, and do not fear me, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God they accuse of indifference is coming in person, preceded by a messenger, and his coming will purify his people like a refiner’s fire and judge those who wrong the weak. They asked, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17). The answer is better, and more frightening, than they expected.

Behold, I send my messenger. First a messenger to prepare the way, like the men who went ahead of a king to clear the road. Some four centuries later John the Baptist appeared in the desert in his camel’s hair, and Mark opened his Gospel by quoting this verse about him (Mark 1:2), together with Isaiah 40:3, introducing both under Isaiah’s name. Jesus said of John, “This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face’” (Matthew 11:10). Malachi has before me; the Gospels have “before your face”, the Father speaking to his Son.

The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. It is his temple, and the one who comes is the Lord himself. Haggai had promised that the glory of this second temple would surpass the first (Haggai 2:9); here is how: the Lord himself will come into it.

The messenger of the covenant in whom you delight. He brings and embodies God’s covenant. And there is a gentle irony in in whom you delight: they say they want God to show up, with no idea what they are asking.

Who can endure the day of his coming? Both questions expect the answer “nobody”, at least on our own record. Two homely pictures show what he will do. A refiner’s fire melts metal to burn off what is mixed into it. Fullers’ soap was the harsh lye cloth-workers used to scour grease out of new wool. Both are violent processes, and both aim at cleaning, not destroying.

He will sit as a refiner. The small word sit matters. A silversmith sits beside the crucible and does not leave it, because metal left too long in the fire is ruined. God gives his full attention to the refining of his people, and he knows exactly how long is enough.

He will purify the sons of Levi. Refining begins with the priests whose corruption filled chapters 1 and 2: God’s cleansing starts with those who handle holy things. (The ESV notes the end of verse 3 may be read “and they will belong to the LORD, bringers of an offering in righteousness”.)

Then I will draw near to you for judgment. Here is the God of justice they asked for, a swift witness. Sorcery, adultery and perjury, yes; and in the same breath, cheating the hired worker of his wages and wronging the widow, the fatherless and the sojourner. Such wrongs seldom came to court, but God has seen them and will testify himself. The root of it all is and do not fear me.

When he came, God came. The messenger is John (Matthew 11:10), so the Lord who came after him to his temple, the messenger of the covenant, is Jesus. He came to it as a baby in Simeon’s arms (Luke 2:22–32), came again to cleanse it (John 2:14–16), and will come again to judge. Before the list of verse 5 none of us stands on our own record. But the Lord who comes to his temple is the one who stood in our place, so for those he has made his own, the fire he brings is the refining of verse 3: they are purified, not consumed.

The refiner at work now. Christians may read their own hard seasons in the light of verse 3. Peter says our trials test faith as fire tests gold (1 Peter 1:6–7), and the Refiner sits by the crucible; he is not careless with his people’s pain. And verse 5 keeps faith honest: the way we pay workers and treat widows, orphans and immigrants is a matter of whether we fear God.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish tradition commonly identifies the messenger who prepares the way with Elijah, promised by name in 4:5, and understands the Lord who comes to his temple as God himself coming in judgment; some also link the messenger of the covenant with Elijah, for whom a chair is set at every circumcision. Both readings agree that a forerunner comes first and then the Lord himself. This commentary’s view: the forerunner is John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10), and the Lord’s coming is the coming of Jesus to his temple (Luke 2:22–32), so that when he came, God came.
verseByVerse.note: In the Hebrew Bible this chapter runs on to the end of the book; English Bibles, following the Greek and Latin, number 3:19-24 as 4:1-6.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s unchanging faithfulness is the only reason his people survive, and he invites them to come back and trust his generosity. Because he does not change, the children of Jacob are not consumed, though they have strayed since their fathers’ days: “Return to me, and I will return to you” (vv. 6–7). When they ask how, he names something concrete. They are robbing him in tithes and contributions, and the whole nation is under a curse (vv. 8–9). So he invites them to bring the full tithe and test him, to see whether he will not open the windows of heaven, rebuke the devourer and make them a land of delight (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's unchanging character is why his people survive, and he invites them to test his generosity by being generous.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed. From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from my statutes and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts. But you say, 'How shall we return?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only God’s unchanging faithfulness has kept his straying people from destruction, and he still invites them home: “Return to me, and I will return to you.”

I the LORD do not change. God’s unchangeableness is not an abstract doctrine here but the reason his people are still alive. If his love depended on his mood or their performance, this generation would have been finished long ago. Because he does not change, the promise made to Jacob still stands over Jacob’s descendants, however disappointing they are. James says the same: with God “there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17).

Return to me, and I will return to you. The same invitation Zechariah had brought to their grandparents (Zechariah 1:3). God keeps saying it.

How shall we return? The reply may be genuine bewilderment, or the defensive shrug of people who cannot think of anything they need to change. Given the tone of the book, the second is likely. God’s answer is wonderfully specific: start with your money (v. 8).

What it means to return. Return is the Old Testament’s great word for repentance, and it is a picture rather than a feeling: someone walking away from God turns round and walks back. God does not say “return to my rules” but Return to me: repentance is coming home to a person. How shall we return? is the voice of people who never noticed they had left, because they had been at the temple all along. And the promise, I will return to you, has a face. In the parable, while the son was still a long way off, the father “ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20); in history, Christ suffered “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). Returning may begin, as in Malachi, with something as concrete as a bank statement, but above all, tell him plainly where you have drifted, and come back to him. See Repentance in the Theological Dictionary.

Does God never change his mind, then? Scripture sometimes says God relented, as when Nineveh repented at the preaching of Jonah (Jonah 3:10). That is the unchanging God responding to people who have changed: he always spares the repentant and always opposes the proud. His nature, purpose and promises do not change (Numbers 23:19).

Shouldn’t God keep up with the times? Our culture tends to assume that change is progress, as if the newest view must be the truest, and so an unchanging God sounds like a problem. But think what a God who kept up with us would be. He would bend to every fashion, approve whatever each age approved, and never be able to tell it anything it did not already think. He would also, Malachi says, be terrifying: a God whose mood shifted with ours would long ago have given up on a people as disappointing as Jacob’s children. The unchanging God is not the enemy of the modern person; he is the only one whose love does not rise and fall with how we are doing. “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end” (Lamentations 3:22). And that love has a face: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8), the same now as he was at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Will man rob God? Yet you are robbing me. But you say, 'How have we robbed you?' In your tithes and contributions. You are cursed with a curse, for you are robbing me, the whole nation of you. Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house. And thereby put me to the test, says the LORD of hosts, if I will not open the windows of heaven for you and pour down for you a blessing until there is no more need. I will rebuke the devourer for you, so that it will not destroy the fruits of your soil, and your vine in the field shall not fail to bear, says the LORD of hosts. Then all nations will call you blessed, for you will be a land of delight, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By withholding the tithe, the whole nation is robbing God and the people his gifts were meant to feed; he invites them to bring it in full and see how generous he is.

Will man rob God? The question is almost comic: who would try to rob God? And the answer is that they are doing it, the whole nation of you.

In your tithes and contributions. Under the law a tenth of the produce supported the priests and Levites, who had no land, along with the poor (Numbers 18:21; Deuteronomy 14:28–29). When the tithe stopped, the ministry starved and the poor went without: not a technicality but theft with victims. Nehemiah found exactly this. The Levites’ portions had not been given, so they had gone back to their fields, until all Judah again brought the tithe into the storehouses (Nehemiah 13:10–12).

Put me to the test. Scripture ordinarily forbids putting God to the test (Deuteronomy 6:16), which makes this invitation rare. The promise is agricultural: the windows of heaven opened means rain, and the devourer rebuked (probably a crop-destroying pest, ESV note) means harvests that survive.

Rich, yet poor for your sake. What moves Christian giving is not a promised return but Christ himself: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The God who opened the windows of heaven for a farming nation has opened heaven itself for us, at the cost of his Son.

What it does not mean. This passage is often misused. It is not a formula for personal wealth. God is addressing a farming nation under the covenant of Moses, promising national harvests for national obedience. To turn it into a guarantee that individual donors will get money back is to promise something God has not promised, and it has done real damage to real people.

What it does teach. Do not flinch from it either. God notices what we do with money; stinginess toward his work is robbery; and he is extravagantly generous, until there is no more need. The New Testament does not lower the standard but changes the motive: “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

The real test. The test God offered Israel was not “give and get rich” but “trust me with what is mine and see whether I let you down”. Christians who give in faith find him just as faithful, though not always in money (Philippians 4:19; 2 Corinthians 9:8). And for believers who are poor and can give little, Jesus counted the widow’s two small coins as more than all the rest (Mark 12:41–44); a gift is acceptable “according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12).

Where Christians differ: does the tithe bind Christians today? Some teach that believers must give exactly a tenth to the church. This commentary’s view: Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.
verseByVerse.note: The “devourer” is probably a crop-destroying pest (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the complaint that serving him is pointless by listening to those who fear him and promising to claim them as his own. Some have said it is vain to serve God, since the arrogant prosper and evildoers escape (vv. 13–15). But those who feared the LORD spoke with one another, and he paid attention: a book of remembrance was written before him (v. 16). They will be his treasured possession, spared as a father spares a son who serves him (v. 17), and the day will come when the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between those who serve God and those who do not, is plain to all (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: God listens to the conversations of those who fear him and writes them down.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your words have been hard against me, says the LORD. But you say, 'How have we spoken against you?' You have said, 'It is vain to serve God. What is the profit of our keeping his charge or of walking as in mourning before the LORD of hosts? And now we call the arrogant blessed. Evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people’s hardest words against God are that serving him does not pay, which shows that they had been serving him for profit all along.

It is vain to serve God. The last dispute, and the most honest thing they say in the whole book: What is the profit? They had kept the rules and gone about as in mourning, fasting and sorry for their sins, and it had not paid. Meanwhile the arrogant were doing very nicely. It is the complaint of Psalm 73, and of every believer who has watched the unscrupulous prosper.

What is the profit of our keeping his charge? Note the assumption buried in profit. They served God as an investment, and they are unhappy with the returns. The relationship was commercial all along, which is why God’s love in 1:2 meant nothing to them.

Religion as an investment. What is the profit? sounds like the voice of doubt, but it is really the voice of religion. These people had kept the rules in order to get something, and when the returns were poor they felt cheated. Their irreligious neighbours, the arrogant, were chasing the same prizes by a more direct route. One group used God to get comfort and success; the other did without him to get the same things. Both were trying to be their own saviours. It is the question Satan asked about Job: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (Job 1:9). Do we love God, or what he gives? The test comes exactly when, as here, serving him seems not to pay.

God himself is the reward. The gospel’s answer is not that serving God pays after all, though it does. It is that God himself is the reward, and a son does not serve his father for wages (v. 17). In Christ he has given not a better return but himself. The psalmist who first made this complaint came out of it saying, “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25). Religion bargains with God; the gospel receives him.

A searching question. Any Christian who feels God owes them a better life might ask: what exactly did we think we were signing up for? The blessings of serving God are enormous, but most of them are not the prosperity these people were looking for.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD and esteemed his name. "They shall be mine, says the LORD of hosts, in the day when I make up my treasured possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him. Then once more you shall see the distinction between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While others grumble, those who fear the LORD encourage one another, and God listens, records it, and promises to claim them as his treasured possession and spare them as his children.

Those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. In the middle of all the grumbling comes a lovely verse. We are not told what they said. They were probably encouraging each other to keep going, reminding one another of God’s promises, refusing the cynicism around them.

A book of remembrance. Heaven was listening: The LORD paid attention and heard them. Kings kept records of loyal service, and God keeps one too; what he writes down is not great achievements but the conversations of ordinary believers who feared him and esteemed his name.

They shall be mine. Treasured possession goes back to Sinai, where God called Israel his own treasure among all peoples (Exodus 19:5). Peter uses the same language of the church, “a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).

As a man spares his son who serves him. A father does not treat his working son as a hired hand. God’s people are not staff; they are family.

The distinction between the righteous and the wicked. Their complaint was that there is no visible difference between serving God and not serving him. God does not deny that it looks that way now. He says the day is coming when the distinction will be unmistakable, and the next chapter describes it.

The Son who was not spared. The New Testament shows what that sparing cost: God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Because the true Son was not spared, the sons and daughters who belong to him will be, and their names are written in the book of life (Philippians 4:3).

In everyday life. Two Christians encouraging each other after a discouraging church meeting, a phone call between friends about the goodness of God: that is what goes into the book. In a cynical season, the simplest faithful act may be to seek out another believer and talk about the Lord, as Hebrews urges: “exhort one another every day” (Hebrews 3:13).

3.title: Behold, I Send My Messenger
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 ended with the people asking, “Where is the God of justice?” This chapter gives God’s answer (vv. 1–5), then holds the fifth dispute, about robbing God (vv. 6–12), and most of the sixth, about whether serving God is worth it (vv. 13–18).

The message. The God they accuse of indifference is coming in person, preceded by his messenger, and his coming will refine his people like silver and judge those who wrong the weak. Because he does not change, they have not been destroyed, and he still says, “Return to me, and I will return to you.” Those who serve him are not wasting their lives: he hears them, writes their names in his book, and will claim them as his treasured possession.

Why it was said. The people were tired and disillusioned: God seemed absent, the harvests were poor, and the wicked prospered (see the introduction). They had stopped bringing the tithes that supported the Levites and the poor, and some had concluded that serving God was pointless.

How the chapter makes its case. God promises a messenger to prepare his way, and then the Lord himself coming suddenly to his temple like a refiner’s fire, to purify the priests and to judge those who oppress the hired worker, the widow, the fatherless and the sojourner (vv. 1–5). Only his unchanging faithfulness has kept them from being consumed, and he invites them to return (vv. 6–7). When they ask how, he names their robbery in tithes and invites them to test his generosity (vv. 8–12). Then he answers the complaint that it is vain to serve him (vv. 13–15): those who fear him speak together, he listens and records it, and a day is coming when the difference between those who serve him and those who do not will be plain (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. By promise, more directly than anywhere else in the book. Jesus said the messenger was John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10), so the Lord who came after him to his temple was Jesus himself: when he came, God came. He is the refiner who purifies a people for himself, and the unchanging LORD of verse 6 is the one of whom Hebrews says, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). The treasured possession spared “as a man spares his son” is the people for whom God “did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:32).

For us. The answer to our doubts about God’s justice is not an argument but a person who has come and will come again. Return to him wherever you have drifted, give to his work as one who trusts him, and when serving him seems not to pay, remember that he is listening and writing it down.
3.theology:
God answers cynicism about his justice by announcing that he is coming himself, preceded by a messenger, fulfilled in John the Baptist (v. 1; 2:17; Mark 1:2). His coming purifies rather than merely destroys; he sits over the refining with full attention, and he begins with those who handle holy things (vv. 2-3). Cheating a worker of his wages stands beside sorcery and adultery in his list, and the root of all of it is not fearing him (v. 5).

His unchanging character is the reason his people are not consumed (v. 6; Jas 1:17; Heb 13:8). Withholding from his work is robbery with victims, and he invites his people to prove his generosity, though not as a formula for personal wealth (vv. 8-12; 2 Cor 9:7). Serving God as an investment leads to disappointment with the returns (vv. 13-15), but he listens to those who fear him, writes their conversations in a book of remembrance, and spares them as a father spares his son, his treasured possession (vv. 16-17; Exod 19:5; 1 Pet 2:9).
3.examples: A road crew is sent ahead of a king four hundred years early. A silversmith sits by the crucible and does not walk away, and harsh soap scours the grease out of new wool. Unpaid wages are listed alongside sorcery and adultery, and God makes a rare invitation: test me on this one. People who served God as an investment are unhappy with the returns, while two believers encourage each other and heaven writes it down.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple
keyVerse.note: This is God’s answer to “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17): not an explanation but an arrival. The Gospels quote it of John the Baptist, so the Lord who came after him to his temple is Jesus. Everything else in the chapter, the refining, the call to return and the book of remembrance, depends on this coming.

3.reflection:
The people asked, “Where is the God of justice?”, and God answered that he was coming, like a refiner’s fire (2:17; 3:1–2). How does the coming of Jesus answer that question? What does the picture of a refiner sitting by the crucible say about God’s purposes in our hard seasons?

“For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed” (v. 6). How does God’s unchanging character comfort you? Why might it also unsettle a culture that assumes change is progress?

God named the people’s giving as the place where their return should begin (vv. 7–10). Why is money such a revealing test of the heart? How should Christ’s generosity (2 Corinthians 8:9) shape the way we give?

Some said, “It is vain to serve God” (v. 14), while those who feared the LORD spoke with one another and God wrote it down (v. 16). When has serving God seemed not to pay for you? Who could you encourage this week, and how?

The day that is coming shall set them ablaze, says the LORD of hosts, so that it will leave them neither root nor branch.<sup>2</sup>But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings.
