verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Day Burning Like an Oven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day that is coming will be a furnace for the arrogant and a sunrise for those who fear God. It will burn the arrogant and evildoers like stubble in an oven, leaving neither root nor branch (v. 1). But for those who fear his name the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and they will go out leaping like calves released from the stall (v. 2). The wicked who seemed untouchable will be ashes under their feet on the day when God acts; his people do not bring that day about, they wait for it (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The same day that burns the arrogant rises like sunshine on those who fear God's name.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven, when all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble. The day that is coming shall set them ablaze, says the LORD of hosts, so that it will leave them neither root nor branch. But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall. And you shall tread down the wicked, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet, on the day when I act, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coming day will burn up the arrogant completely, but for those who fear God it will be a sunrise that brings righteousness, healing and joy. This is the day of 3:18, when the difference between the righteous and the wicked becomes unmistakable. (In Hebrew Bibles these verses are 3:19–21.)

Burning like an oven. The picture is a clay oven heated white with burning straw. The arrogant, the very people the complainers had called blessed (3:15), are the stubble that goes in. Neither root nor branch means nothing left to grow again.

Judgment and love. The Bible is unembarrassed about this, and love does not require us to be embarrassed either. A world where cruelty and arrogance were never finally dealt with would not be a kinder world.

The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. The book’s last great promise. The same day that burns like an oven rises like the sun for you who fear my name: not a furnace but a sunrise. The dawn does not merely announce that night is over; it brings warmth and life, and this one brings righteousness, its rays spreading across the sky like wings and carrying healing. A winged sun was a familiar emblem in the ancient world, including the Persian empire that ruled Judah, but this sun is the LORD’s, and its wings bring healing. Every believer who has come out of long spiritual darkness knows what this verse feels like.

You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall. Anyone who has seen cattle let out after a winter indoors knows the picture: awkward, delighted, kicking, running for no reason except that they can. That is God’s description of his people on that day: not a solemn procession, but calves let out of the shed.

You shall tread down the wicked. The wicked, who had seemed untouchable, become ashes, on the day when I act. God’s people do not bring this about, and they are not told to. They wait.

The sunrise from on high. Zechariah the priest, holding his newborn son John, prophesied that “the sunrise shall visit us from on high” to give light to those who sit in darkness (Luke 1:78–79). The sun rose in Bethlehem, and Charles Wesley taught the church to greet it every Christmas: “Hail the Sun of Righteousness!” Christ is the righteousness this sun brings, and the healing in its wings is his, which is why the same day can be a furnace for some and a sunrise for others: the difference is whether we are found in him.

Where Christians differ: does this teach annihilation? The burning of stubble pictures the total, final ruin of the wicked, and some Christians read it, with similar texts, as their ceasing to exist. This commentary’s view: Jesus speaks of “eternal punishment” (Matthew 25:46), and Revelation of torment that goes on for ever (Revelation 14:11). The image describes the completeness of judgment, not its end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Remember Moses, and Elijah Is Coming
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With prophecy about to fall silent, God tells his people to hold fast to his word and to watch for the forerunner he will send. They are to remember the law he gave Moses at Horeb (v. 4). And before the great and awesome day of the LORD he will send Elijah the prophet (v. 5), who will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and of children to their fathers, so that the land is not struck with utter destruction (v. 6). The Old Testament ends looking back to Moses and forward to Elijah, and both would one day stand beside Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology: The Old Testament closes by pointing back to Moses and forward to the forerunner of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the law of my servant Moses, the statutes and rules that I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel. "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As prophecy falls silent, God tells his people to hold fast to the law he has already given, and promises to send Elijah before his great day to turn hearts back and avert the curse.

Remember the law of my servant Moses. The first instruction is to remember the law (the ESV notes the last phrase may read “and just decrees”), given at Horeb to a people God had already brought out of Egypt. Hold on to what you already have. That is God’s regular provision for his people in quiet seasons: not new revelations but faithful attention to the word he has given.

I will send you Elijah the prophet. The second is a promise: Elijah, not necessarily the man himself but one in his mould, the prophet who confronted a whole nation’s idolatry on Mount Carmel. Centuries later, an angel told an old priest that his son would “go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah … to make ready for the Lord a people prepared” (Luke 1:17). Jesus said of John the Baptist, “if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14), and later, “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him” (Matthew 17:12).

He will turn the hearts of fathers to their children. The book ends in the home. The last work described before the coming of the Lord is not a political revolution or a temple ceremony but hearts turned between fathers and children. In Malachi’s day the homes were breaking: men were leaving the wives of their youth (see the note on 2:13–16), and Nehemiah found children of mixed marriages who could not speak the language of Judah (Nehemiah 13:23–24). A nation is renewed one household at a time, and a revival that leaves families cold has not gone deep.

Strike the land with a decree of utter destruction. The final words are heavy. The ESV notes that the phrase refers to what is devoted to the LORD for destruction. Our English Old Testament closes on the word “destruction”, with a warning still hanging in the air and nothing yet done about it; the synagogue, finding the ending so stark, repeats verse 5 after verse 6 when the book is read.

Moses and Elijah. The book’s last two names meet again on a mountain. When Jesus was transfigured, Moses and Elijah appeared talking with him, and the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:3–5). The Law and the Prophets stood beside the one they had pointed to.

The silence, and the curse lifted. Some four centuries passed with no new prophet. Kingdoms rose and fell, and God’s people waited without knowing what they were waiting for. Then John appeared in the wilderness in a garment of camel’s hair, calling a nation to repent and pointing to someone coming after him. The messenger of 3:1 had arrived, and behind him came the Lord to his temple. The curse hanging over the last verse of the Old Testament was not lifted by better behaviour. It fell on him: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The book that begins with I have loved you and ends with a threatened curse is answered by a cross, and ever since, those set free by it have gone out like calves let out of the stall.

For the fatherless. Where fathers have failed, God is “Father of the fatherless” (Psalm 68:5), and the gospel that turns hearts can begin with yours, whatever your father was like.

How do I remember his word? In Scripture to remember is to keep something before you and act on it, not merely to recall it. Read it regularly. A plan that takes you steadily through the whole Bible keeps you from living on a few favourite verses. Store some of it. Learn a verse a week, on the commute or at the sink: “I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). Hear it with God’s people. Sit under faithful preaching on the Lord’s Day and talk about it afterwards. Pass it on at home. Malachi ends with fathers and children, and Moses said, “You shall teach them diligently to your children” (Deuteronomy 6:7): a psalm at the table, a child’s question answered from the Bible. Read it toward Christ. On the Emmaus road, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Read that way, the law no longer only accuses us; it points us to the one who kept it in our place.

Do these laws apply to Christians? Christians are not under the law of Moses as a covenant (Romans 6:14; Galatians 3:24–25), but it remains Scripture, “profitable for teaching” (2 Timothy 3:16). The Reformed tradition reads it in three strands. Its moral law, rooted in God’s character and creation and repeated in the New Testament, still binds (Romans 13:8–10). Its ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, clean and unclean, feasts) was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1). Its civil law governed Israel as a nation under God and ended with that theocracy, though its principles of justice still teach us.

Was John the Baptist Elijah? John denied being Elijah in person (John 1:21), which is what his questioners meant; Jesus said he was the Elijah Malachi promised, coming in Elijah’s spirit and power (Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14). Both are true. It gives no support to reincarnation.

Where Christians differ: is the promise of Elijah wholly fulfilled? Most Christians take it as fulfilled in John. Some expect a further Elijah-like ministry before Christ’s return, reading Matthew 17:11 that way. This commentary’s view: Jesus’ words that Elijah “has already come” (Matthew 17:12) point to John as the fulfilment, and all agree that the one whose way was prepared is Jesus Christ.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish tradition expects Elijah himself, who was taken up and never died (2 Kings 2:11), to return before the Messiah; at Passover a cup is poured for him and the door opened, and the Mishnah (Eduyot 8:7) says he will come to make peace in the world. Both readings agree that Elijah’s coming means the Messiah is near. This commentary’s view: it follows Jesus, who said that John the Baptist was the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12), and so believes that the One he announced has already come and will come again.

4.title: The Sun of Righteousness
4.overview:
Where we are. This short chapter (in Hebrew Bibles, the end of chapter 3) finishes the sixth dispute and closes the book, and with it the Old Testament prophets. Chapter 3 ended with God’s promise that one day the difference between those who serve him and those who do not would be plain; this chapter describes that day.

The message. The day of the LORD is coming, and it will be two things at once: a furnace for the arrogant and a sunrise for those who fear his name. Until it comes, God’s people are to hold fast to the word he has already given, and to watch for the messenger he will send in the spirit of Elijah to turn hearts back before he comes.

Why it was said. The complainers of 3:14–15 said that the arrogant prosper and serving God is vain (see the introduction). God answers with the end of the story, and then, with no new prophet to follow for some four centuries, tells his people what to do while they wait.

How the chapter makes its case. The coming day will burn the arrogant and evildoers like stubble, leaving neither root nor branch (v. 1). But for those who fear his name the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and they will go out like calves let out of the stall (vv. 2–3). Meanwhile they are to remember the law of Moses (v. 4), and to look for Elijah, who will come before the great day to turn the hearts of fathers and children, lest the land be struck with utter destruction (vv. 5–6).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need it leaves open. The angel said that John would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17), and Jesus said that John was the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14). John’s father sang that “the sunrise shall visit us from on high” (Luke 1:78). Moses and Elijah, the book’s last two names, stood with Jesus on the mountain of his transfiguration. And the curse on which the Old Testament ends fell on Christ, who “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

For us. We live after the sunrise and before the full day. Hold fast to the Scriptures, let the gospel turn your heart toward your family, and wait for Christ’s return not with dread but with the joy of calves let out into the sun.
4.theology:
The final day deals with arrogance and evil completely, and a world in which that never happened would not be kinder (v. 1). The same day is a furnace to the arrogant and a sunrise to those who fear God's name: Christ is the sun of righteousness who rises with healing, and the right picture of his people then is calves let out of the stall (vv. 1-2). They do not bring the day about; they wait for it (v. 3).

In seasons when God seems silent, his provision is faithful attention to the word already given (v. 4). He prepared the way for his coming by sending a messenger in the spirit of Elijah, fulfilled in John the Baptist (v. 5), and the renewal he looks for reaches into the home (v. 6). The curse that hangs over the last verse of the Old Testament fell on Christ.
4.examples: An oven is heated white with burning straw, while a sunrise spreads its rays like wings, carrying healing, and cattle are let out of the shed after a long winter. Before the silence falls comes a final instruction, remember what you already have, and a promise of a prophet in Elijah's mould who would arrive four hundred years later and exactly on time. Revival reaches as far as the kitchen table, and an Old Testament that ends on the word “destruction” is answered by a cross.

keyVerse.quote: But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall.
keyVerse.note: The same day that burns the arrogant like stubble rises like the sun on those who fear God. It answers the complaint that serving God is vain (3:14): his people’s end is healing and joy. The New Testament hears the dawn of this sunrise in the birth of Christ (Luke 1:78).

4.reflection:
The same day is a burning oven for the arrogant and a sunrise for those who fear God (vv. 1–2). Why is it good news that evil will finally be dealt with? How does knowing Christ change the way you think about that day?

“You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall” (v. 2). How does this picture of joy challenge the way we often imagine the end, or the Christian life now?

As prophecy fell silent, God told his people to “remember the law of my servant Moses” (v. 4). What helps you keep God’s word before you in quiet or dry seasons?

The Old Testament ends with hearts turned between fathers and children (v. 6). What would it look like for the gospel to turn hearts in your family, or in the families of your church?
